paragraph: “JOHN, WHOSE SURNAME WAS MARK” (ACTS 12:12) · CALLED IN ACTS 12

blocks.text: “JOHN, WHOSE SURNAME WAS MARK” (ACTS 12:12) · CALLED IN ACTS 12
John Mark. Son of a Jerusalem household where the church prayed; left the first journey, and was later “profitable” to Paul.
ALSO CALLED
John · Mark · Marcus (KJV, Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24; 1 Peter 5:13)
FROM
His mother Mary had a house in Jerusalem where “many were gathered together praying” the night Peter was freed from prison.
TRADE
Scripture does not say
FAMILY
His mother was Mary, at whose house the believers met.
WRITINGS
The Gospel according to Mark (its traditional title)
BACKGROUND
Home, trade and family
FROM
FAMILY
His mother was Mary, at whose house the believers met. Acts 12:12
From the textPaul calls him “sister's son to Barnabas” in the KJV; the Greek word is rendered “cousin” in the Revised Version (1881). Colossians 4:10
From the textScripture never names his father. Acts 12:12

Scholars' viewPeter calls him “Marcus my son” (1 Peter 5:13). Smith (1884) takes it that Mark “probably owed his conversion” to Peter; MacRory (1910) that the word “need not be taken to imply more than affectionate regard for a younger man”. 1 Peter 5:13 [16][19]
THE CALLING
Called, as 2 accounts tell it
“took with them John, whose surname was Mark.”
Acts 12:25 (KJV) →
WHERE HE WENT
Acts and after
Dashed pins are places known only from later tradition, not from Scripture.
Jerusalem · His mother's house; where he went back from Perga. Acts 12:12 Acts 13:13
Antioch (Syria) · Brought here by Barnabas and Saul; where Paul and Barnabas parted over him. Acts 12:25 Acts 15:35–37
Salamis · Serving Barnabas and Saul on Cyprus. Acts 13:5
Paphos · The party sailed from here to Perga. Acts 13:6 Acts 13:13
Perga · Where he left them. Acts 13:13
Cyprus · Sailed there with Barnabas. Acts 15:39
Colossae · Paul expected he might come to the church there. Colossians 4:10
Babylon (1 Peter 5:13) · no map pin · Where Mark was with Peter; whether this is Rome by a figure or another city is disputed, so no pin is drawn.
Rome (in tradition) · tradition · Clement of Alexandria (about 200): Mark wrote down Peter's preaching at Rome.
Alexandria (in tradition) · tradition · Eusebius (about 325), “they say”: Mark founded the church there; Jerome (392): buried there.
IN ACTS AND THE LETTERS
Peter, freed from prison by the angel, went to the house of “Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark”. Acts 12:12
He went with Barnabas and Saul through Cyprus, but at Perga in Pamphylia “John departing from them returned to Jerusalem”. Acts 13:4–13

When Barnabas wanted to take him on the second journey, Paul refused, since he “departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work”; Barnabas took him and sailed to Cyprus. Acts 15:36–39

Later he is with Paul while Paul is “in bonds”, and Paul tells the Colossians to receive him if he comes; he is one of the few “of the circumcision” who are Paul's “fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God” and “a comfort” to him. Colossians 4:3 Colossians 4:10–11
Paul names him among “my fellowlabourers” in the letter to Philemon. Philemon 1:24
In 2 Timothy Paul writes: “Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.” 2 Timothy 4:11
Peter sends greetings from “The church that is at Babylon … and so doth Marcus my son”. 1 Peter 5:13

From the textColossians and Philemon do not say where Paul was imprisoned, and which city 1 Peter 5:13 means by “Babylon” is disputed (see the Letters page for 1 Peter). Colossians 4:10 Philemon 1:23–24 1 Peter 5:13
COMPANIONS
Who was with him
Each line joins him to someone Scripture places beside him.
Mary, his mother Her house in Jerusalem was a meeting place of the church. Acts 12:12
Barnabas His relative; took him to Antioch, on the first journey and to Cyprus. Acts 12:25 Acts 15:37–39 Colossians 4:10
Paul Took him on the first journey, refused him for the second, and later called him a fellow-worker and “profitable to me for the ministry”. Acts 13:5 Acts 15:38 Colossians 4:10–11 2 Timothy 4:11
Peter Came to his mother's house after his escape; sends greetings from “Marcus my son”. Acts 12:12 1 Peter 5:13
Aristarchus With him and Paul in the greetings of Colossians and Philemon. Colossians 4:10 Philemon 1:24
Jesus called Justus Named with him as one of Paul's Jewish fellow-workers. Colossians 4:10–11
Luke Named with him among Paul's fellow-labourers; “Only Luke is with me”, Paul writes when he asks for Mark. Philemon 1:24 2 Timothy 4:11
Demas Named with him among Paul's fellow-labourers. Philemon 1:24
Timothy Asked to bring Mark with him to Paul. 2 Timothy 4:9–11
Silvanus Named with him at the close of 1 Peter. 1 Peter 5:12–13
HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
From the textScripture does not record Mark's death. His last mentions are 2 Timothy 4:11 and 1 Peter 5:13; which of the two is later is not known. 2 Timothy 4:11 1 Peter 5:13
TRADITION SAYS

“And they say that this Mark was the first that was sent to Egypt, and that he proclaimed the Gospel which he had written, and first established churches in Alexandria.”[1][2] Who says so: Eusebius, Church History 2.16.1, about AD 325

“When Nero was in the eighth year of his reign, Annianus succeeded Mark the evangelist in the administration of the parish of Alexandria.”[1] Who says so: Eusebius, Church History 2.24, about AD 325; Nero's eighth year is AD 62 (McGiffert)

“He died in the eighth year of Nero and was buried at Alexandria, Annianus succeeding him.” MacRory (1910) thinks this is probably drawn from Eusebius, and notes that if Mark was alive when 2 Timothy was written he cannot have died in 61-62. 2 Timothy 4:11 [3][19] Who says so: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 8, AD 392

The Acts of Mark give him a martyr's death, dragged through the streets of Alexandria. MacRory: “we have no evidence earlier than the fourth century that the saint was martyred”, though he adds that this silence “is not at all decisive against the truth of the later traditions”.[19] Who says so: The Acts of Mark, as reported by MacRory (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910), no earlier than the 4th century
Venetians later carried his remains from Alexandria to Venice; Farmer (ISBE, 1915) gives the year as 815.[21][19] Who says so: Venetian tradition, as reported by Farmer (ISBE, 1915), 9th century
WRITINGS
Writings tied to him
READ
The Gospel according to Mark (its traditional title)
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
One man

Eusebius (about 325) and Jerome (392), who join the Gospel's Mark to Peter's “Marcus my son”; A. C. McGiffert (1890); Smith (1884); Easton (1897); MacRory (1910), who says the identity “is not questioned by any ancient writer of note”

The Mark of Colossians is Barnabas's relative, and Acts ties John Mark closely to Barnabas; the Mark Peter calls his son fits the son of Mary, at whose house Peter took refuge. Colossians 4:10 Acts 15:37–39 Acts 12:12 1 Peter 5:13 [1][3][2][16][15][19]
Several men

The list “On the Seventy Apostles” among the doubtful works of Hippolytus (date unknown, “Probably spurious, but yet antique”); the Greek church's calendar, which MacRory notes keeps a feast of Mark the evangelist on 25 April and of John Mark on 27 September
That list names three: “Mark the evangelist, bishop of Alexandria”, “Mark, cousin to Barnabas, bishop of Apollonia”, and “Mark, who is also John, bishop of Bibloupolis”.[11][19]
IN SCRIPTURE
Every passage
CHAPTERS · 7
Acts 12 Acts 13 Acts 15 Colossians 4 Philemon 1 2 Timothy 4 1 Peter 5
PASSAGES · 8
Acts 12:12–17 Acts 12:25 Acts 13:4–13 Acts 15:36–39 Colossians 4:10–11 Philemon 1:23–24 2 Timothy 4:9–11 1 Peter 5:12–13
WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture never names Mark's father, says how he came to believe, or says why he left at Perga.
The Gospel of Mark does not name its writer; the link to this Mark comes from Papias and later writers.
Scripture does not say where Paul was imprisoned when he wrote of Mark in Colossians and Philemon, or record how or where Mark died.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON

From the textActs calls him “John, whose surname was Mark” (12:12, 25; 15:37), then just “John” (13:5, 13), then “Mark” (15:39); Paul and Peter write “Marcus” or “Mark” (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11; 1 Peter 5:13). Our person data holds all of these as one man; whether they are is a question below. Acts 12:12 Acts 12:25 Acts 15:37 Acts 13:5 Acts 13:13 Acts 15:39 +4 more

Early church · Eusebius (trans. A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 1), 1890Papias, early in the 2nd century, passes on from “the presbyter” that Mark became “the interpreter of Peter”. The Gospel that bears his name does not name its writer.[1]

Early church · Hippolytus (trans. J. H. MacMahon and S. D. F. Salmond, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5), 1886Hippolytus, early in the 3rd century, calls him “Mark, he of the maimed finger”. MacRory (1910) lists the explanations later offered: that he cut off his thumb to unfit himself for the priesthood, that his fingers were naturally short, or that the word is a figure for “deserted”.[11][19]

Later tradition · Joseph MacRory, 1910The preface to his Gospel in manuscripts of the Latin Vulgate calls him a Levite who had served as a priest in Israel. MacRory notes that early writers are silent and that it may be “only an inference from his relation to Barnabas the Levite”. Our person data also gives him the tribe of Levi. Acts 4:36 Colossians 4:10 [19]
